impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner who licenses exclusive rights to a licensee but retains the right to sue third parties for infringement retains sufficient exclusionary rights to establish constitutional standing to bring an infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains the right to sue for infringement—even after granting an exclusive license—possesses a sufficient exclusionary right to satisfy Article III standing. The court emphasized that the retained right to sue was not rendered illusory by the rights granted to the licensee.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring exclusive licenses can retain standing to enforce patents by preserving the right to sue independently for infringement, providing flexibility in licensing arrangements while maintaining enforcement capability.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patents claiming methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's patents covering methods of treating headache with humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies, after a jury had found willful infringement and no invalidity. This decision has major implications for pharmaceutical patent scope, particularly for genus claims covering classes of biologic drugs.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies may benefit from broader patent protection for biologic drug classes, as the court upheld patent claims covering a genus of humanized antibodies despite only one specific antibody being disclosed in the specification.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors like Eli Lilly face renewed risk of infringement liability for their competing anti-CGRP antibody products, potentially affecting market access for biosimilar or competing biologic treatments.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court's jury instruction and verdict form regarding patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 were legally flawed, and whether a single infringement question covering all asserted patents on the verdict form was reversible error.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated an $11.5 million patent infringement judgment and remanded for a new trial, finding that the verdict form's use of a single question covering infringement for all four asserted patents was error because it prevented meaningful appellate review. The court also remanded the § 101 eligibility analysis for the '495 patent under Alice step two.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from clearer requirements that verdict forms must separately address infringement for each asserted patent, enabling more effective appellate review of multi-patent cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased risk of vacatur when verdict forms aggregate infringement findings across multiple patents, requiring more detailed jury instructions and verdict forms that increase trial complexity and cost.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied inter partes review estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting invalidity grounds that were not raised in its IPR petition but that a skilled searcher reasonably could have discovered.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve, holding that the lower court relied on insufficient evidence to estop one invalidity ground and failed to adequately account for hindsight bias when estopping another. The decision clarifies the evidentiary standard for determining what prior art a 'skilled searcher' could have reasonably discovered.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent litigation benefit from a higher bar for applying IPR estoppel, preserving the ability to assert invalidity defenses that were not included in prior IPR petitions where the evidence of discoverability is weak.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater difficulty in invoking IPR estoppel to limit defendants' invalidity defenses, potentially leading to broader and more costly validity challenges in district court litigation.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using passive data collection devices were patent-ineligible abstract ideas under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in finding the case was not exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming-data patents were directed to patent-ineligible subject matter under § 101 but vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional, potentially opening the door for attorney fee awards to the defendant. The decision reinforces the difficulty of patenting data collection and processing methods in agricultural technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of infringing data-aggregation patents in agriculture and similar industries benefit from continued strong application of § 101 eligibility challenges, and the remand on exceptionality may deter assertion of weak patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies seeking patent protection for automated data collection and processing systems face heightened patent eligibility risks, limiting the enforceability of software-implemented agricultural technology patents.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to support the jury's finding that each of the four asserted trade secrets was a protectable trade secret under California law, and whether the inventorship challenge to defendants' patents should have been sustained.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, holding that the plaintiff failed to demonstrate its asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying information was generally known. The court also reversed on patent invalidity, finding the purported inventive contribution mirrored the generally known information. The counterfeiting claim and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from the court's rigorous application of the requirement that trade secrets must not be generally known, providing a strong basis for challenging insufficiently defined or publicly available alleged trade secrets.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection for product designs and manufacturing processes must ensure their claimed trade secrets are clearly defined and demonstrably not generally known in the industry, or risk having misappropriation claims dismissed.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate designee may testify at summary judgment to matters beyond personal knowledge, and whether the on-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that a sale expressly disclose the functionality of the prior art device.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of patent invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that a 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify beyond personal knowledge at the summary judgment stage and that the on-sale bar does not require that a commercial sale expressly disclose the prior art device's internal functionality. The decision clarifies evidentiary standards at summary judgment in patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants challenging patents can more effectively use 30(b)(6) testimony and prior commercial sales to establish the on-sale bar, even when the witnesses lack personal knowledge or the sales did not disclose internal functionality.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face an expanded scope of the on-sale bar, as prior commercial sales of devices embodying claimed inventions may invalidate patents even without public disclosure of the device's underlying functionality.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly granted summary judgment of noninfringement of a multi-core processor patent based on extraterritoriality and rejection of VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory, and whether the court properly struck certain damages expert theories.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the grant of summary judgment of noninfringement of the '836 patent, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding VLSI's infringement theories, while affirming in part. The decision addresses the extraterritorial reach of U.S. patent law for multi-core processor technology and the scope of permissible damages theories in high-value semiconductor patent disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the semiconductor industry benefit from the court's willingness to find genuine disputes of material fact on infringement, keeping high-value claims alive for trial and limiting premature dismissal.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies like Intel face continued exposure to substantial patent infringement claims involving processor technology, with the reversal requiring further proceedings that extend costly litigation.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's damages expert testimony and in its assessment of trade secret damages models, and whether the court properly reduced the jury's breach of contract damages award.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the reduction of the jury's breach of contract award, reinstating it. The case involves Ford's alleged misappropriation of automotive configuration software trade secrets after expiration of a license agreement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors benefit from the court's reinstatement of jury-awarded contract damages and the instruction to reconsider broader damages models for trade secret misappropriation, potentially increasing recovery in licensing disputes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal replacements for licensed software face significant trade secret misappropriation risk and damages exposure, with the court affirming liability and expanding the range of permissible damages theories.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Insulet's Defend Trade Secrets Act claim was time-barred by the three-year statute of limitations, where the alleged misappropriation began in 2018 and suit was filed in 2023.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's denial of JMOL and held that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred, finding that the statute of limitations had expired before suit was filed. The case involved a medical device competitor hiring former employees who allegedly shared proprietary CAD files and design information for insulin patch pumps.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations, providing certainty about when potential claims expire and limiting exposure to stale allegations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must be diligent in monitoring potential misappropriation and filing suit promptly, as delay beyond the three-year limitations period will bar recovery even where misappropriation is substantiated by evidence.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated eligibility rulings for certain patent claims involving non-uniform constellations used in digital broadcast systems but affirmed eligibility for others, while also affirming infringement and damages findings. The decision provides important guidance on the patent-eligibility boundary for signal-processing innovations embedded in communication standards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies holding patents on signal-processing innovations in communications standards benefit from the court's affirmance of eligibility for certain claims and the denial of JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer electronics manufacturers like LG face continued patent infringement exposure for products implementing digital communication standards, with the court upholding substantial damages findings.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action after it missed the deadline for seeking a stay of the original action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the mandatory stay deadline under § 1659(a)(2) by voluntarily dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action. The decision prevents gamesmanship in parallel ITC and district court proceedings involving pharmaceutical patent disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders pursuing ITC investigations benefit from the court's anti-gamesmanship holding, which prevents respondents from manipulating the mandatory stay provision to delay district court proceedings.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the statutory deadline for requesting a mandatory stay of parallel district court litigation cannot cure the missed deadline by refiling their action, potentially forcing them to litigate on two fronts simultaneously.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether the patent holder was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the finding of no literal infringement and no infringement by equivalents for Actelion's epoprostenol pharmaceutical composition patents, holding that the pH claim limitation refers to measurement at a field-standard temperature. The decision has significant implications for Hatch-Waxman ANDA litigation and claim drafting for pharmaceutical formulation patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers benefit from precise claim construction that narrows pharmaceutical composition patents, facilitating market entry for generic versions of branded drugs like Veletri.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders face narrower claim scope when using technical parameters like pH without specifying measurement conditions, potentially undermining patent protection for drug formulations.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB erred in its obviousness determination for patent claims directed to sensor-based logistics systems with time-delayed reporting, and whether a non-party to underlying litigation may file an IPR petition on behalf of a litigant to circumvent the one-year time bar under 35 U.S.C. § 315(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness finding for FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings. The case raised significant questions about potential abuse of the IPR system when a non-party files petitions challenging patents asserted against a different entity, timing the filing to coincide with the real party in interest's statutory deadline.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from increased scrutiny of potential proxy IPR petitions, protecting against manipulation of the one-year time bar by parties not directly involved in underlying litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to use IPR proceedings face greater risk that petitions filed by apparent proxies will be scrutinized for real-party-in-interest issues, potentially limiting strategic use of the IPR system.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may correct patent inventorship under 35 U.S.C. § 256(b) when the omitted coinventor cannot be located, and whether the patents are invalid for failure to name all inventors.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the patents were invalid due to the omission of a coinventor who could not be located. The court held that § 256(b) correction was unavailable because the patent holder failed to demonstrate sufficient diligence in locating the missing coinventor, and the error in inventorship could not be excused under the circumstances.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent infringement cases can leverage inventorship challenges as a complete defense to invalidity where coinventors from foreign collaborators or contractors are omitted and cannot be located.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that collaborate with foreign manufacturers on product development must ensure all contributors to the invention are properly identified and contactable, or risk patent invalidation for incorrect inventorship.
